{
 "id": "Q03",
 "sourceFile": "Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-injure.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-injure' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine"],
 "sports": ["American Football", "Track & Field", "Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Collegiate", "Injured Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional analysis of routinely collected data from a prospective cohort of 60 NCAA Division I athletes (11 women) from American football, track and soccer who had an index hamstring strain injury. Eccentric hamstring strength was tested with the NordBord at return to sport; 8 athletes (13%) re-injured the same limb within 1 month and 11 (18%) within 3 months. Strength, total force and between-limb asymmetry did not differ between athletes who did and did not re-injure (p values 0.47 to 0.96).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 8 and 11 re-injuries were observed, so the study had little power to detect a difference, and one strength test per athlete was taken at varying times after return. Prior injury history was incomplete, and mild and severe injury groups could not be analysed.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the null result as meaning return-to-sport eccentric testing does not predict re-injury, when the sample is small and the study tests one time point per athlete.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Kocak UZ, Stiffler-Joachim MR, Heiderscheit BC. Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-injure. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2023;59:25-29.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.11.006",
  "abstract": "Eccentric hamstring strength and between-limb asymmetry were measured at return to sport in 60 collegiate athletes after a first hamstring strain, and compared between those who did and did not re-injure within 1 and 3 months.",
  "tldr": "Eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry measured at return to sport did not separate athletes who re-injured from those who did not. A single return-to-sport NordBord result should not be used alone as a re-injury screen based on this study.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional analysis of routinely collected data from a prospective observational cohort at one university. Eccentric hamstring strength was measured with the NordBord, typically within 7 days of return to sport. Re-injury was a new strain to the same limb within 1 or 3 months of return, and groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests.",
  "findings": "Of 60 athletes, 8 (13%) re-injured within 1 month and 11 (18%) within 3 months. Injured-limb, uninjured-limb and total peak eccentric force did not differ by re-injury status (p 0.47 to 0.75 in Table 2), and median asymmetry was 8.2% vs 7.8% at 1 month and 8.3% vs 7.1% at 3 months (p 0.91 and 0.96). Asymmetry was also similar within the moderate-severity subgroup (p 0.89 and 0.79).",
  "limitations": "The study had very few re-injuries, timing of testing relative to return varied, prior injury history was incomplete, and mild and severe subgroups were not analysed. Conflict in the source: the Results text gives asymmetry p values of 0.43 or higher, while Table 2 and the abstract give 0.91 and 0.96; the table values are reported here.",
  "practicalImplications": "In this sample, eccentric strength and asymmetry at return to sport did not identify athletes at higher re-injury risk, so a normal score should not be read as proof of low risk. The authors suggest the test is still useful for tracking an injured athlete's strength development.",
  "athleteDev": "Use eccentric strength testing to track an individual's rehab progress, but do not treat a return-to-sport score as a predictor of re-injury, since asymmetry did not separate re-injured from non-re-injured athletes here.",
  "rtp": "Strength and asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between athletes who re-injured and those who did not within 3 months. The study cannot set an RTS threshold, so it should not be used as a clearance criterion."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q04",
 "sourceFile": "Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise - Introduction to an Emerging Concept.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise: Introduction to an Emerging Concept' matches the filename (the running head says 'Connected').",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative leading article that reviews resistance equipment (free weights, weight stacks, bands, isokinetic machines and flywheels) and practitioner surveys, then introduces connected adaptive resistance exercise (CARE) for accentuated eccentric and eccentric-only training. Preliminary data come from one machine: a laboratory example, and usage records from 100 men in non-laboratory settings (2,124 sets and 18,174 repetitions) showing higher eccentric than concentric loads. The authors conclude that CARE technology appears feasible in lab and non-lab settings but that formal studies of effectiveness are still required.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The data are descriptive usage records with no controls, reliability, validity or outcome measures, and two authors were previously employed by Vitruvian, the maker of the machine described. The review methods are not described, so it is not a systematic review.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the preliminary loading data as evidence that CARE machines build strength better than established equipment, when the paper reports no training outcomes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Nuzzo JL, Pinto MD, Nosaka K. Connective Adaptive Resistance Exercise (CARE) Machines for Accentuated Eccentric and Eccentric-Only Exercise: Introduction to an Emerging Concept. Sports Medicine. 2023.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-023-01842-z",
  "abstract": "This leading article introduces connected adaptive resistance exercise (CARE), which adjusts resistance in real time to the person's own force, as a way to deliver accentuated eccentric and eccentric-only exercise. It reviews equipment limits and shows preliminary data from one machine.",
  "tldr": "CARE machines adjust resistance in real time, which may make eccentric overload and eccentric-only sets practical without spotters or releasers. There are no outcome studies yet, so treat them as an emerging option rather than a proven upgrade.",
  "methods": "Narrative leading article. The authors summarise practitioner surveys and the mechanical limits of free weights, weight stacks, bands, isokinetic machines and flywheels, then describe one CARE machine (Trainer+). Preliminary data come from a laboratory biceps curl example and from usage records of 100 men in non-laboratory settings.",
  "findings": "The machine's algorithm delivered higher eccentric than concentric loads, with an eccentric:concentric strength ratio of 1.42 across 18,174 eccentric-concentric repetitions and 4.99 for eccentric-only repetitions in the usage data. Loads fell automatically as strength declined, giving drop-set-like sets. The authors cite earlier validation work reporting strong correlations (r of at least 0.94) with dumbbell one-repetition maximum.",
  "limitations": "The authors state that formal reliability, validity and effectiveness studies of CARE machines for muscle size, strength or clinical outcomes are limited. The usage data are descriptive, uncontrolled, and drawn from a machine made by a company whose former employees are authors.",
  "practicalImplications": "Where a CARE device is available, it can deliver eccentric overload and eccentric-only sets without a spotter, with loads adjusting as the athlete fatigues. Until outcome studies exist, use it as one delivery option alongside established methods rather than as a proven replacement.",
  "athleteDev": "For strength work, CARE-type machines may allow eccentric overload and automatic drop sets without a spotter, which could suit athletes who train alone or in small gyms. This paper does not show greater strength or power gains than existing methods.",
  "rtp": "This paper reports no rehabilitation or injury outcomes. The authors suggest CARE machines may suit clinical or telehealth eccentric work, but this cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q05",
 "sourceFile": "Copenhagen five second squeeze a     valid indicator of sports related hip and groin function.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Copenhagen five-second squeeze: a valid indicator of sports-related hip and groin function' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Validation study in 667 sub-elite male football players at the start of the season (construct validity), with responsiveness and floor and ceiling analysis in 52 players reassessed later in the season and test-retest reliability in 10 players. The five-second squeeze pain score (0-10) correlated with the HAGOS Sport score (Spearman rho -0.61, p<0.01) and with change in HAGOS Sport (rho -0.51). Test-retest concordance was 0.90 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.97), and median HAGOS Sport scores were 97, 69 and 47 for pain scores 0-2, 3-5 and 6-10.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Reliability rests on 10 players and responsiveness on 52, so the confidence intervals are wide, and the sample is sub-elite and male. The pain-based traffic-light cut-offs were not tested against injury, re-injury or return to play, and the post hoc subgroup analyses were small (24 and 15 players).",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat a score of 6 or more as a clearance decision on its own, when the paper proposes a traffic-light approach that has not been validated for predicting injury or return to play.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Thorborg K, Branci S, Nielsen MP, Langelund MT, Hölmich P. Copenhagen five-second squeeze: a valid indicator of sports-related hip and groin function. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51:594-599.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2016-096675",
  "abstract": "The authors tested whether a five-second hip-adduction squeeze, rated on a 0-10 pain scale, reflects sport-related hip and groin function in football players. They assessed validity in 667 sub-elite male players, responsiveness in 52 and test-retest reliability in 10.",
  "tldr": "The five-second Copenhagen squeeze, with a pain rating, tracks sport-related hip and groin function in footballers and needs no equipment. In this cohort, a pain score of 6 or more went with substantially impaired function.",
  "methods": "Construct validity was assessed cross-sectionally in 667 players at baseline. Responsiveness and floor and ceiling effects were assessed in 52 players with a later clinical examination, and test-retest reliability in 10 stable players whose score changed by 10 points or less. Analyses used Spearman correlations, Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney tests and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, following COSMIN and STROBE.",
  "findings": "Squeeze pain correlated with HAGOS Sport (rho -0.61) and with the other HAGOS subscales (rho -0.51 to -0.60), all p<0.01. Change scores correlated with HAGOS Sport change (rho -0.51). Test-retest concordance was 0.90 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.97). HAGOS Sport medians were 97, 69 and 47 for pain scores 0-2, 3-5 and 6-10, and floor or ceiling effects were present in 4 of 39 symptomatic players.",
  "limitations": "Reliability and responsiveness rest on small subsets, and the sample is sub-elite and male. Players may under-report pain because a high score can mean stopping play, and the subgroup correlations were post hoc.",
  "practicalImplications": "A five-second squeeze with a pain rating can be added to routine screening with no equipment. A score of 6 or more flags a player for clinical review before play, and the authors suggest the 0-2, 3-5 and 6-10 bands can act as traffic lights that need testing against outcomes.",
  "athleteDev": "Use the squeeze as a quick, equipment-free check of groin function in squad screening and track the score over the season. Players scoring 6 or more showed large functional deficits, so review them before loading them in training.",
  "rtp": "The squeeze is a responsive monitor of groin function, which may help show progress during rehabilitation. It does not test return-to-play decisions, and its traffic-light thresholds have not been validated against re-injury or outcomes after return."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q06",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of cold-water immersion compared with other recovery modalities on athletic performance following acute strenuous exercise in physically.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants' matches the filename (the filename is truncated).",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression of 28 studies (searched from inception to 12 September 2022) in athletes or physically active people, comparing cold-water immersion (CWI) with active recovery, contrast water therapy, warm-water immersion, air cryotherapy and massage. CWI reduced muscle soreness compared with other methods at 24 h (effect 0.29, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.56) and 48 h (0.31, 0.05 to 0.57), but not at 1 h. Pooled effects on power, strength, flexibility and creatine kinase were not significant, and air cryotherapy was better than CWI for immediate power and for strength.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most stratified comparisons rest on few small studies with low or very low GRADE certainty and high heterogeneity, and crossover and parallel designs were pooled with an adjustment. Several included studies were judged low quality, and the review does not cover injured athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "The abstract calls CWI superior for muscle soreness, but the benefit is small and appears at 24 and 48 hours, not at 1 hour, where the effect was trivial and not significant.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Moore E, Fuller JT, Bellenger CR, et al. Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression. Sports Medicine. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-022-01800-1",
  "abstract": "This systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression pooled randomised trials comparing cold-water immersion with other recovery methods after strenuous exercise in physically active people. Outcomes covered soreness, power, strength, flexibility, creatine kinase and perceived recovery at 1 to 96 hours.",
  "tldr": "Cold-water immersion reduces muscle soreness compared with other recovery methods at 24 and 48 hours, with small effects. It does not clearly improve power, strength or flexibility overall, and air cryotherapy outperforms it for strength and immediate power.",
  "methods": "Searches of seven databases to 12 September 2022 for peer-reviewed English-language trials in people competing or physically active who had a strenuous exercise bout followed by CWI or another recovery method. Risk of bias was assessed with the SIGN RCT checklist, data were pooled as Hedges' g with random-effects models, and GRADE was used to rate certainty. Water temperature and duration were tested as meta-regression moderators.",
  "findings": "Twenty-eight studies were meta-analysed. CWI reduced soreness versus other methods at 24 h and 48 h, while the 1 h effect was trivial and not significant. Overall effects on power, strength, flexibility and creatine kinase were not significant. Air cryotherapy was significantly more effective than CWI for power at 1 h (effect -0.70, p=0.03 in the stratified analysis). Temperature and duration were not significant moderators, except for power at 24 h compared with active recovery.",
  "limitations": "Many comparisons rest on few small studies with low or very low GRADE certainty and high heterogeneity, and the review pools crossover and parallel designs. The abstract's general claim that CWI is superior for soreness rests on the 24 and 48 h effects, not the 1 h result, which was not significant.",
  "practicalImplications": "After a single hard session, cold-water immersion is a reasonable option for soreness, with the benefit most evident 24 to 48 hours later. Do not expect it to speed recovery of strength or flexibility, and note the authors' warning that it may blunt adaptations to resistance training during preparation phases.",
  "athleteDev": "Cold-water immersion may reduce next-day soreness after hard sessions, but the authors warn it may blunt resistance-training adaptations during preparation phases, so avoid routine use after strength work aimed at gains.",
  "rtp": "This review covers recovery after induced exercise stress in physically active people, not injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. Its findings cannot be applied to injury rehabilitation."
 }
}

input.content:
{
 "id": "Q07",
 "sourceFile": "Effects of external pneumatic compression device vs static compression garment on peripheral circulation and markers of sports performance and recovery.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Effects of an External Pneumatic Compression Device vs Static Compression Garment on Peripheral Circulation and Markers of Sports Performance and Recovery' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": ["Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized parallel-group trial in 30 healthy, active young men (age 23 years, exercising at least 3 days a week) who completed 100 drop jumps and were then randomized to 30 minutes of partial-leg external pneumatic compression (EPC), static compression socks (SC) or no treatment (CTL). Jump height, isokinetic torque, soreness and pressure-pain threshold did not differ between conditions. Squat-jump relative propulsive force and power were higher in EPC and SC than CTL at 24 and 48 h, and EPC kept countermovement-jump braking measures stable over time while values fell in CTL.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Thirty men, one treatment and one follow-up schedule, with no between-condition difference in jump height or isokinetic torque, so the benefit is limited to some relative jump force and power measures. The braking result is a within-group pattern, not a between-group difference, and the trial does not test repeated use or athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the abstract as showing that EPC improves jump performance, when jump height did not differ and EPC was no better than static compression socks.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Blumkaitis JC, Moon JM, Ratliff KM, et al. Effects of an external pneumatic compression device vs static compression garment on peripheral circulation and markers of sports performance and recovery. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2022;122:1709-1722.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s00421-022-04953-z",
  "abstract": "Thirty healthy, active men did 100 drop jumps and then received a 30-minute partial-leg pneumatic compression treatment, static compression socks or no treatment. Soreness, blood flow, jump and isokinetic measures were followed for 48 hours.",
  "tldr": "After a damaging drop-jump session, one 30-minute partial-leg pneumatic compression treatment did not change jump height or soreness compared with control. It did help keep some squat-jump force and power higher at 24 and 48 hours, with results similar to static socks.",
  "methods": "Randomized parallel-group trial in 30 healthy, active men who did 100 drop jumps, then received EPC, SC or CTL for 30 minutes. Soreness, pressure-pain threshold, blood flow, muscle thickness, circumference, isokinetic torque, and countermovement and squat jump force and power were measured before, after treatment, and at 24 and 48 h, analysed with mixed-factor ANOVA.",
  "findings": "Jump height, isokinetic torque, soreness, pressure-pain threshold, blood lactate and limb size showed no condition effects. Squat-jump relative propulsive force was higher in EPC and SC than CTL at 24 h and 48 h, and squat-jump relative propulsive power was higher in both at 24 and 48 h, with EPC also higher at 30 minutes. For countermovement jumps, EPC kept relative braking force and braking power stable over time, while CTL values fell.",
  "limitations": "The trial had 30 men, one treatment and short follow-up, and it does not show effects in athletes or with repeated use. The abstract says EPC maintained braking force across time points, which describes within-group change; no between-condition difference in braking force was found.",
  "practicalImplications": "Partial-leg pneumatic compression after a damaging jump session may help some people keep squat-jump force and power up to 48 hours later, but it did not change jump height or soreness. It was no better than static compression socks, so the choice can rest on cost and comfort.",
  "athleteDev": "Pneumatic compression after a hard jumping session may help keep squat-jump output more consistent over the next two days, but in this trial static socks did about as well, so cost and comfort should guide the choice.",
  "rtp": "The trial used healthy, active men after induced muscle damage, so it cannot inform return-to-sport or injury rehabilitation decisions."
 }
}
